COURSE DESCRIPTION
This course provides a behavioral decision science toolkit for solving real-world problems in business and policy
practices. In organizations, managers often rely on personal experience, anecdotes, and organizational beliefs to set
strategies intended to have an effect. This course discusses ways in which strategies that may appeal on an intuitive
level can be challenged and improved by behavioral sciences, and transformed in order to gain a competitive edge.
Students will apply scientific principles to learn how and why suboptimal decisions are taken in business
and in public policymaking. In considering real-world problems, this course will discuss research in the fields of
behavioral economics, consumer and organizational behavior, social and cognitive psychology, and experimental
political science related to how people make judgments and decisions.
Along the way, students will learn how to design and test actionable interventions. To be fully equipped
with the principles of behavioral science, studying those principles alone is not sufficient. Undertaking research—
learning how to test, and actual implementation—are also needed. The course content is designed to help students
to experience interventions, and to learn how to put them to test. They will gain fresh perspectives on marketing
strategies, managerial practices, and financial decisions, with “actionable” and “tangible” knowledge.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
• Understand the principles of behavioral sciences behind challenges found in business and public policy
• Evaluate the potential effectiveness of real-world interventions
• Create effective real-world interventions to change people’s behavior based on behavioral sciences
ASSESSMENT METHODS
Discussion Leading as a Team: 20%
Quiz (3 quizzes, 15% each): 45%
Term-paper (Group Project): 35%
TOTAL: 100%
DETAILS OF ASSESSMENT METHODS
• Team-based In-Class Exercise: Starting from Lesson 3, groups of three students (except for one week when
there will be a group of four due to the class size) will be assigned the role of discussion leaders. The task
of the discussion leaders is to present real-world cases where the findings of behavioral sciences as
reported in the assigned readings are seemingly (1) replicated or (2) refuted.
The discussion leaders are strongly encouraged to meet outside of class and plan for leading the
discussion. You may use any audio or visual materials (such as PowerPoint slides, YouTube videos) that
you think will advance the discussion or everyone's understanding of the material. Each student (as a
team) will lead the discussion once during the course.
To ensure fair assessments of the team-based exercises, a group will be formed by random selection. To
help the teams of discussion leaders, the instructor will hold a group consultation meeting via Zoom on
Saturdays at 7:30 pm.
• Comprehensive Quiz: There will be 3 quizzes during this class. These will be announced quizzes based on
the prior meeting’s lecture and reading materials. They will assess students’ comprehension on the
learned materials, as well as the ability to apply the learned principles to the relevant contexts. Each quiz
will contain 15 multiple-choice questions. Students will be given 25 minutes to complete the quiz.
• Term paper (Group Project)
: The goal of this term paper is to give students practice with—and to test their
mastery of—the course material. With the rise of agentic AI products and systems, there is also growing
opportunity to use such tools to apply what students have learned to building products of their own. In
Week 6, at the midpoint of the semester, students will learn how to rapidly prototype digital products
intended to serve as decision architecture. Building on this, students need to (a) analyze which principles
are relevant and pertinent to a given digital product of interest, and then (b) build an improved version of
its decision architecture that achieves the intended effects.
